lawyer:
Dr M Zahir with Moqbul Ahmed, Advocates  ----- For the Petitioner.
Mostafa Zaman Islam, Assistant-Attorney-General  ----- For Respondent No. 1
parties:
Didarul Kabir (Md) ----- Petitioner
Vs
Commissioner of Customs and others  ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Syed Amirul Islam J: In this Rule the petitioners have challenged the imposition of separate customs duties and other taxes on its various equipment, in addition to the taxes and duties levied on the vessel itself on its LDT. Further, the assessment has also been questioned as customs duties and other charges along with VAT have been calculated on the basis of tariff value instead of auction price.

2. The petitioner No. 1 is the auction purchaser of the vessel MV Alexandra and after purchase of the ship when the respondents demanded customs duties on the basis of Annexures "D" and D (1) the petitioner No.1 moved this Court and obtained the instant Rule. During pendency of the Rule the petitioner No.1 sold the said vessel to one Alhaj Shamsul Islam Chowdhury who has subsequently been added in this Rule at his instance as co-petitioner No.2.

3. The short fact of the case is that, the petitioner No. 1 participated in an international tender for auction sale of vessel MV Alexandra. The said tender was invited pursuant to an order dated 9-12-97 passed by the High Court Division in Admiralty Suit Nos. 46 of 1996 and 61 of 1997. The auction sale was held on 20-1-98 when several bidders including the petitioner No.1 participated and petitioner No.1 's bid was found to be the highest at Taka 1,05,00,000 (Taka one crore five lac) only. The offer of the writ petitioner No.1 was considered to be sufficient and was accepted by the Marshal subject to confirmation by this court. This Court ultimately confirmed the said auction and thereafter the Registrar of the High Court Division by a letter dated 11-3-98 asked the petitioner No.1 to comply with all the formalities, terms and conditions of the auction sale and to make payment of tax, etc and port dues against vessel MV Alexandra. After the confirmation of the auction sale the respondent No.1 assessed customs duties on the vessel and on some other items as evidenced by Annexures "D" and D(1) and made a demand of Taka 1,48,93,941.21 on account of customs duties vide Memo No. S/13/ AIN/Mongla/96/97 /-98/19806, dated 3-4-98 asking the petitioner No.1 to deposit the said duties whereupon the petitioner No.1 moved this Court and obtained the instant Rule.

4. Dr M Zahir, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, submits that the petitioners have purchased the vessel in question in auction sale and therefore) the petitioners are entitled to pay customs duties on the vessel itself and the customs authority most illegally and without jurisdiction assessed the customs duties on the vessel as well as on some other components of the vessel as evidenced by Annexure D(1). The learned Advocate further submits that making the demand pursuant to Annexure D(1) is also illegal and not tenable in law. Dr Zahir further submits that as per SRO No. 173/ Ain/97 /1723/ Custom, dated 8-7- 1997 the rate of import duty of vessel and other floating structures for breaking up which is covered by HS Code No. 8908 is fixed at 7.5% ad valorem, but in the instant case the customs authority have levied customs duties at the said rate on the basis of Tariff Value ignoring the auction price which is also illegal and without jurisdiction. Dr Zahir further submits that it is evident from the confirmation order passed by the Admiralty Court that the ship had no steering and it was in a very miserable and dilapidated condition and her condition was rapidly deteriorating and the vessel was burnt by fire twice and as a result of which all engine bearings, pumps, electrical system were totally damaged beyond repair and the vessel at that time had no crew member on board resulting in damage to navigable equipment and safety equipment and therefore the respondents have committed an illegality in assessing the customs duties on the basis of Tariff Value ignoring all these vital aspects of the matter. Dr Zahir further submits that since the vessel in question was purchased in auction direct through this Court the customs authority was obliged to levy customs duties on the auction price and not on the basis of the Tariff Value. Dr Zahir also submits that the respondents by making assessment of the ship violated the provisions of section 27 of the Customs Act inasmuch as they have not taken into consideration the essential fact that the ship has been damaged by file which fact was very much known to the respondents. The final submission of Dr Zahir is that admittedly the petitioners have purchased the vessel in auction and the relevant HS Code is HS Code No. 8908.00.10 for which the petitioners are liable to pay customs duties at the rate of 7.5% ad valorem but the customs authority in addition to that also assessed ten other items on different HS Code and levied customs duties although they are the integral parts of the ship in question.

5. Mr Mostafa Zaman Islam, the learned Assistant Attorney-General appearing for the respondent No.1, submits that the selfsame question which has been raised in this writ petition earlier also were raised in two other writ petitions, namely, Writ Petition No. 1693 of 1997 and 1479 of 1999 and in Writ Petition No. 1479 of 1999 a Division Bench of this Court held that for vessels which are sold in auction for scrapping after the beaching of the said vessels certain parts are removable from the ship which are liable to be levied with customs duties under the relevant HS Code and for the LDT (Light Displacement Tonnage) the ship is levied with customs duties on the basis of LDT and in Writ Petition No. 1693 of 1997 it was held by a Division Bench of this court that the customs authorities are entitled in law to levy customs duties on items which  are not included in LDT. The learned Assistant Attorney-General further submits that the question of tariff value also came up for consideration in the said Writ Petition No. 1479 of 1999 wherein it was held by a Division Bench of this Court that Government has legally determined tariff value for vessels and other floating structures for breaking up and therefore, the customs authorities did not commit any illegality in assessing the customs duties on individual items and also on the basis of LDT for the vessel itself on the basis of tariff value. The learned Assistant Attorney- General further submits that section 27 of the Customs Act has no manner of application in the instant case inasmuch as the petitioner purchased the vessel at a point of time when it was not sea- worthy. It was an arrested vessel which had no crew on board and had been damaged by fire twice and knowing full well that the ship itself is a damaged unseaworthy ship they have participated in the tender only with a view to scrap the ship and section 27 of the Customs Act is not attracted.

6. Dr M Zahir when confronted with the aforesaid two judgments submitted in reply that in Annexure D(1) ten items, namely, item Nos. 1-10 have been separately charged to customs duties under different HS Codes but except item Nos. 5 and 7 the other 8 items are integral parts of the ship and therefore, they cannot be separately classified and no customs duty can be realised for those items separately.

7. In this case mainly two questions have been raised by the petitioners in relation to levy of customs duties. Their first contention is that inauction they have purchased a vessel which is covered by HS Code No. 8908.00.10 and they are liable to pay duties under that HS Code for the vessel in question on the auction price and not on the tariff value fixed by the Government for such item. The selfsame question earlier came up for consideration in an unreported case before this Court, namely, in Writ Petition No. 1479 of 1999. The facts of that case are very much similar to the facts of the instant case. In that case also the auction purchaser challenged the imposition of customs duties on the basis of tariff value and the vires of the SRO by which tariff value was fixed by Government for such item was challenged. A Division Bench of this court consisting of Mr Justice Mohammad Fazlul Karim as his Lordship then was, and Mr Justice MA Wahhab Miah held that the fixation of tariff value was legal and valid and held that in view of the SRO No. 70/99/Cus, dated 15-2-99 being prevalent at that time fixing tariff value of the scrap vessel on the basis of LDT under HS Code No. 8908.00.10 the scrap vessel was liable to be assessed with customs duty, VAT and other charges on the basis of tariff value fixed by the said SRO.

<u>8. In the instant case auction took place on 20-1-98 and it was confirmed on 13-3-98. But in the application it is not mentioned when the bill of entry was presented. However, from Annexure 'D'(1) it appears that the assessment was made on 29-3-99. SRO No. 42/93 Customs, dated 25-3-98 was published in the gazette on 31-3-98 and it came into force from 25-3-99. Before that SRO No. 33/97/Cus dated 30-12-97 was in force with effect from 30-12- 97 till 24-3-98 and in both the aforesaid SROs the scrap vessel (LDT) under HS Code No. 8908.00.10 has been fixed with tariff value at the rate of US Dollar 175.00 per metric ton. From Annexure "D"(1) it is clear that the assessment was made on 29-3-99. Therefore, the bill of entry must have been submitted on or before 29-3-99. Whatever be the date of presentation of the bill of entry, since 30-12- 97 the tariff value was 175.00 US Dollar per metric ton for scrap vessel and therefore, the customs authority have not committed any illegality in assessing the Customs duty on the tariff value which was prevalent on the date of presentation of the bill of entry. The petitioner has failed to establish that the tariff value was not fixed objectively rather their case is that since they have purchased the vessel in auction, the assessment of Customs duties and other taxes should be made on the basis of auction price and not on the basis of tariff value. It is now well settled that whatever be the auction price, the vessel will be assessed on the basis of tariff value, if there be any. Thus, we do not find any force and substance in the submission of DrZahir that the Customs authorities have committed an illegality by making the assessment on the basis of tariff value.</u>

<u>9. Now let us advert to the other pertinent question that has been raised by the petitioners. Dr Zahir strenuously argued that the customs authority most illegally and without jurisdiction levied customs duties on at least eight items as enumerated in Annexure "D"(1) out of which except item Nos. 5 and 7 the other items form integral part of the ship. Therefore, they cannot be separately classified and no customs duty can be levied upon them. To resolve this question we may take judicial notice of the fact that when a ship is imported as scrap vessel, it requires a special treatment for allowing the ship for beaching and for its next treatment as scrap vessel. It is essential before any process of examination or the appraisement of the scrap vessel starts. Upon a declaration of import of a scrap vessel, it is allowed for beaching of the scrap vessel as per Government Notification No. 15 dated 24-4-87 and at the time of allowing such beaching the importer is provided with some facilities in the shape of allowing some items as duty-free and integral parts of the scrap vessel for facilitating its beaching and only those items exceeding the numbers mentioned in the said notification and found in the joint inventory' are to be classified under respective HS Code for the purpose of assessment and realisation of customs duties, Vat and other charges as leviable and it may further be noted that before breaking up the ship the importer separates all movable and disposable goods, like furniture, television, motor machine, fuel, light, fittings, etc, and sells out to home consumers without causing any damage or breaking up. Thus the ship in the beach can be separated from all other disposable goods and thereafter the imported vessel is broken up. Here it may further to be mentioned that the Light Displacement Tonnage means LDT in metric tons as per builders registered LDT referred to in the Stability Book or the builders certificate at the time of initial commission of the vessel or the floating structure. Light Displacement Tonnage i.e. LDT, is the gross weight of the constituent materials by which the vessel is built. So, the things other than the constituent materials are not included in LDT. We have already mentioned about the General Notification No. 15, dated 20-4-87 in which mere guidelines have been given for the process of levying duty upon the scrap vessel and to make an inventory of the goods in the said vessel. It may be borne in mind that the ship declared for scrapping is not a ship in running condition and only upon beaching under customs control, the next course of its treatment as scrap vessel starts. When under customs control, the inventory prepared after physical examination in a manner as indicated in the aforesaid notification exposes the list of all including goods having all qualities and utilities of transfer/sale to others inside the country for local consumption and without being scrapped. A seaworthy ship is classified under Chapter 89 and falls under HS Code No. 8901.90 which on import or in running condition stays assembled and complete with all what it holds. But while a ship is imported and declared before the customs fur beaching as scrap vessel, it departs from HS Code No. 8901.90 and merits classification under heading No. 8908 which reads, "Vessels and other floating structures for breaking lip". After beaching, a ship upon declaration as a scrap vessel starts dismantling some of its movable apparatus, engines, etc, which subsequently appear disintegrated, independent and fit for disposal without being scrapped and for which an inventory showing all tile goods including ships intended for scrapping is prepared while the ship is under customs control. Thereafter the importer presents Bill of Entry along with all other documents. So, it is the duty of the Customs authority to determine movable and consumable goods without being scrapped and fit for passing straight on to home consumption and they are classified under their receptive HS Codes and likewise customs duty. VAT, etc is also livable as these goods are not scrapped or broken in a manner the ship is scrapped or broken and, as such, they said notification was issued. Since the ship is built with some constituent materials in the dockyard at the time of building of any ship or vessel, the weight of the ship is considered as LDT i.e. Light Displacement Tonnage and other essential and additional tools and other things are not included in LDT, and altogether the weight of the loaded goods, fuel, weight of the water to keep the empty vessel balanced, weight of the drinking water kept in the ship, weight of the other goods, things and weight of the sailors is called "constant" and when constant and LDT are taken together then it is called "dead weight". The scrap vessel is dutiable item as per Customs Act on the basis of LDT and not on the basis of dead weight of the vessel. The scrap vessel is classified under its proper heading No. 89.08 and other movable and consumable goods are classified under their respective HS Codes. The argument of double taxation does not arise at all because scrap vessel is classified under HS Code 8908.00.10 and other disposable and non-breakable items are classified under their respective HS Codes and customs duty, Vat and other charges are realised as per prevailing rate on the date of filing of the bill of entry.</u>

10. Under Explanatory Notes, Second Edition, 1996.Volume-IV of Harmonised Commodity Description and Coding System issued by World Customs Organisation, Brussels. Heading No. 89.01 is for Cruise ships excursion boats, Ferry-Boats, Cargo ships, Barge and similar vesels for the transport of persons or goods. HS Code 8901-10.10 is for Cruise ship, excursion boats. HS Code No. 8901-10-20 is for ferry boats. HS Code No. 8901.10.30 is for vessels principally designed for the transport of persons of DWT not exceeding 3000 metric tons. The HS Codes continue up to 8901-90-90. Then comes heading No. 89.02 and it includes only one HS Code namely, HS Code No. 8902.00.00 which is for fishing vessels, factory ships and other vessels for processing or preserving fishery products. Heading No. 89.03 is for pleasure or sports, rowing boats and canoes. Heading No. 89.04 is for tugs and pusher craft. Heading No. 89.05 are for light-vessels, fire-floats, dredgers, floating cranes, etc. Heading No. 89.06 is for other vessels, including war ships and lifeboats, other than rowing boats and heading No. 89.07 is for other floating structures like rafts, tanks, cofferdams, landing stages, buoys and beacons. Heading No. 89.08 is for vessels and other floating structures for breaking up. "This heading has two HS Codes HS Code No. 8908.00.10 is for vessels and HS Code No. 8908.90 is for other floating structures for breaking up. This heading is restricted to the vessels and other floating structures of Heading No. 8908 and when presented for the purpose of breaking up, such vessels may be obsolete or damaged and may have had their instruments, machinery, ete removed prior to presentation. In the instant case the petitioners submitted that the scrap vessel LDT is the total weight of the vessel including the belongings and is inclusive of generator and the other items mentioned in Annexure 'D' (1) but, according to the respondents, a vessel is usually built with some constituent materials in the dockyard and at the time of building of any ship or vessel the sight of the ship is considered as LDT (Light Displacement Tonnage). The other essential and additional tools and other things are not included in LDT and that all together with the weight of the loaded goods, fuel, weight of the water to keep the empty vessels balanced, weight of the drinking water kept in the ship, weight of the other goods, things, and weight of the sailors is called "constant" and then when constant and LDT is taken together then it is called "dead-weight". The scrap vessel is dutiable item under the Customs Act on the basis of LDT and not on the basis of dead-weight. We have already seen that HS Code No. 8908.00.10 is for the vessels and HS Code No. 8908.00.90 is for other floating structures for breaking up is restricted to Heading No. 89.08 when presented for the purpose of being broken. Such vessels may be obsolete or damaged and may have had their instruments, machinery, etc. removed prior to presentation. Thus, it is clear that prior to presentation of a scrap vessel LDT for assessment of customs duty, Vat and other charges the instruments and machineries etc are required to be removed and the same are not part and parcel of the scrap vessel which are liable to be assessed on the basis of their respective HS Codes. In that view of the matter it was held by a Division Bench of this Court in Writ Petition No. 1693 of 1997 that only those items which are indispensable and essentially required for beaching are exempted from levy of customs duties but other times are liable to be taxed as per their respective HS Codes.

11. In the instant case we have carefully examined Annexure "D"(1) and on perusal of the same it appears that the items mentioned therein are not integral parts of LDT scrap vessel and are not required for floating and beaching the vessel. These are items which are removable without breaking or dismantling' the ship. They can be removed individually and can be sold in the home market for consumption directly to the consumers. Therefore, it appears, that the customs authorities have rightly assessed customs duties for those items under the relevant HS Code and in doing so they have not committed any illegality whatsoever.

<u>12. One of the other points which have been agitated by the petitioners is that, the Customs Authority committed an illegality in assessing the customs duty on the LDT scrap vessel on the basis of the tariff value. The relevant SRO was produced by the learned Assistant Attorney-General at the time of hearing and the SRO was also examined by Dr Zahir who then found it difficult to press the point any further. There is no dispute that government can fix tariff value for any goods under section 25(7) of the Customs Act and in the instant case tariff value is fixed at the rate of US$175 per metric ton. The basis of the petitioner's claim is that they have purchased the vessel at an auction price of Taka 1,05,00,000 whereas respondent No.1 assessed customs duties at Taka 1,48,93,941.21 on the tariff value of the ship. Since the auction price was approved by this court in the admiralty suit there is no scope to assess Customs duties in the instant case on the basis of tariff value, more so when admittedly the ship is damaged and unseaworthy, is the contention raised by the petitioner. Suffice it to say that it is now well settled that tariff value for any item can be fixed by the government under section 25(7) of the Customs Act and it has so been fixed by the Government though SRO No. 33/97/Cus. dated 30-12-97 and SRO No. 42/93/Cus, dated 25-3-98. It is not the case of the petitioners that without any material basis the tariff value has been fixed. Their only allegation is that as the ship has been purchased through auction held by this court, the customs duties ought to have been assessed on the basis of auction price and not on tariff value. The same question came up earlier for consideration before a Division Bench of this Court in Writ Petition No. 1479 of 1999 wherein also it was argued that the ship having been purchased in auction, the customs duties and other charges ought to have been made on the basis of auction price and not on the basis of the tariff value. This contention was negatived and it was held that customs duties. VAT .and other charges must be paid on the basis of tariff value. We do not find any reason to take a different view, more so when admittedly there is a tariff value for the scrap LDT vessel.</u>

13. Dr Zahir emphatically urged before us that in the instant case section 27 of the Customs Act is applicable and in assessing customs duty and other taxes the respondents ought to have taken into consideration that the ship was damaged and unseaworthy and therefore, ought to have accepted the auction value for making assessment. We have examined the provisions of section 27 of the Customs Act and find that they have no manner of application to the instant case. It is not covered by section 27 of the Act.

14. Accordingly, we do not find any infirmity in the impugned order of assessment and direction to pay the Customs duty and other charges.

15. In the result, the Rule is discharged, however without any order as to cost.

The respondents are at liberty to realise the balance dues by encashing the Bank Guarantee.

End.
